1.o: In this chapter we have, I. David declining in his health, ver. 1-4. II. Adonijah aspiring to the kingdom, and treating his party, in order to it, ver. 5-10. III. Nathan and Bathsheba contriving to secure the succession to Solomon, and prevailing for an order from David for the purpose, ver. 11-31. IV. The anointing of Solomon accordingly, and the people's joy therein, ver. 32-40. V. The effectual stop this put to Adonijah's usurpation, and the dispersion of his party thereupon, ver. 41-49. VI.
1.i: With Adonijah plotting, David has Solomon anointed king at the spring of Gihon, and the people shout for joy.
1.p: Lord, You choose leaders in Your own way. Be with every leader, and give them wisdom. Amen.
1.l: Cheer someone on today who is starting a new job or task, and say, God bless you.
q: Only kings and great men rode mules. What small sign of honor do you give the people who serve you?

2.o: In this chapter we have David setting and Solomon at the same time rising. I. The conclusion of David's reign with his life. 1. The charge he gives to Solomon upon his death-bed, in general, to serve God (ver. 1-4), in particular, concerning Joab, Barzillai, and Shimei, ver. 5-9. 2. His death and burial, and the years of his reign, ver. 10, 11. II. The beginning of Solomon's reign, ver. 12. Though he was to be a prince of peace, he began his reign with some remarkable acts of justice, 1.
2.i: First Kings 2 is a king's deathbed speech, followed by the hard first months of a new reign.
2.p: Lord, You established David's throne. Give wisdom to every young leader, and help us to walk in Your ways. Amen.
2.l: Ask an older person in your family for one piece of advice, and write it down.
q: Caution and circumspection are what keep us steady. Where do you need to slow down and look at where you are walking?

3.o: Solomon's reign looked bloody in the foregoing chapter, but the necessary acts of justice must not be called cruelty; in this chapter it appears with another face. We must not think the worse of God's mercy to his subjects for his judgments on rebels. We have here, I. Solomon's marriage to Pharaoh's daughter, ver. 1. II. A general view of his religion, ver. 2-4. III. A particular account of his prayer to God for wisdom, and the answer to that prayer, ver. 5-15. IV.
3.s: Solomon Asks for a Listening Heart
3.i: In a dream at Gibeon, God offered Solomon anything, and Solomon asked for an understanding heart to govern God's people, so God gave him wisdom and also riches and honor.
3.p: Lord, give us listening hearts. Teach us to ask for what serves others, and to trust You with the rest. Amen.
3.l: Ask God for one thing today that is not for yourself: wisdom to help a friend, or kindness for someone hard to love.
q: Those who love God will not grudge the cost of their religion. What do you give to God that actually costs you something?

4.o: An instance of the wisdom God granted to Solomon we had in the close of the foregoing chapter. In this we have an account of his wealth and prosperity, the other branch of the promise there made him. We have here, I. The magnificence of his court, his ministers of state (ver. 1-6), and the purveyors of his household (ver. 7-19), and their office, ver. 27, 28. II. The provisions for his table, ver. 22, 23. III. The extent of his dominion, ver. 21-24. IV. The numbers, case, and peace, of his subjects, ver. 20-25. V.
4.i: God gave Solomon wisdom greater than all the East and Egypt, shown in his proverbs, songs and knowledge of nature, and people of all nations came to hear him.
4.p: Lord, You are the source of true wisdom. Teach us to know You, and to use what we learn to serve others. Amen.
4.l: Find a short, wise saying in the Bible's book of Proverbs and read it aloud to someone today.
q: Solomon's wisdom drew visitors from many nations. What do others learn by watching how you live?

5.o: The great work which Solomon was raised up to do was the building of the temple; his wealth and wisdom were given him to qualify him for that. In this, especially, he was to be a type of Christ, for "he shall build the temple of the Lord," Zech. vi. 12. In this chapter we have an account of the preparations he made for that and his other buildings. Gold and silver his good father had prepared in abundance, but timber and stones he must get ready; and about these we have him treating with Hiram king of Tyre. I.
5.i: King Hiram of Tyre agrees to supply cedar and pine logs for Solomon's temple in exchange for food.
5.p: Lord, You use people from many places to build Your house. Thank You for friends and partners. Amen.
5.l: Work with someone different from you today on a project, and thank God for what each of you can do.
q: Hiram, a foreign king, praised the Lord for Solomon's wisdom. How can you encourage someone who is doing God's work?

6.o: Great and long preparation had been making for the building of the temple, and here, at length, comes an account of the building of it; a noble piece of work it was, one of the wonders of the world, and taking in its spiritual significancy, one of the glories of the church. Here is, I. The time when it was built (ver. 1), and how long it was in the building, ver. 37, 38. II. The silence with which it was build, ver. 7. III. The dimensions of it, ver. 2, 3. IV.
6.i: Solomon begins to build the temple with stones cut in advance, and the Lord promises to live among His people if they obey.
6.p: Lord, You live among Your people. Build in us a house that honors You. Amen.
6.l: Prepare ahead of time for something important this week, and notice how it makes things go smoothly.
q: God's promise to live among His people depended on their obedience. What does that say about the temple itself?

7.o: As, in the story of David, one chapter of wars and victories follows another, so, in the story of Solomon, one chapter concerning his buildings follows another. In this chapter we have, I. His fitting up several buildings for himself and his own use, ver. 1-12. II. His furnishing the temple which he had built for God, 1. With two pillars, ver. 13-22. 2. With a molten sea, ver. 23-26. 3. With ten basins of brass (ver. 27-37), and ten layers upon them, ver. 38, 39. 4. With all the other utensils of the temple, ver.
7.s: Hiram of Tyre and the Temple Furnishings
7.i: First Kings 7 lists Solomon's buildings and the bronze work of a half-Israelite craftsman from Tyre.
7.p: Lord, You give skill to those who work with their hands. Bless the builders, and let everything we make honor You. Amen.
7.l: Make something with your hands today and do it as well as you can, as a gift for someone.
q: Solomon built for God first and then for himself. What do you build first in your week?

8.o: The building and furniture of the temple were very glorious, but the dedication of it exceeds in glory as much as prayer and praise, the work of saints, exceed the casting of metal and the graving of stones, the work of the craftsman. The temple was designed for the keeping up of the correspondence between God and his people; and here we have an account of the solemnity of their first meeting there. I. The representatives of all Israel were called together (ver.
8.i: Solomon brings the ark into the new temple, God's glory fills the house in a cloud, and Solomon prays.
8.p: Lord, the heavens cannot hold You, yet You hear us. Fill our lives with Your presence. Amen.
8.l: Pray today in a quiet place, and thank God that He hears you wherever you are.
q: Solomon knew a building could not hold God. Where do you meet Him?

9.o: In this chapter we have, I. The answer which God, in a vision, gave to Solomon's prayer, and the terms he settled with him, ver. 1-9. II. The interchanging of grateful kindnesses between Solomon and Hiram, ver. 10-14. III. His workmen and buildings, ver. 15-24. IV. His devotion, ver. 25. V. His trading navy, ver. 26-28.
9.s: The Lord Appears to Solomon Again
9.i: First Kings 9 gives Solomon a second vision, with a promise and a warning, and then lists his building projects and his fleet.
9.p: Lord, You keep Your name among us. Keep our hearts loyal, and let our building and trading serve Your purposes. Amen.
9.l: Think of one promise you have made, and ask God to help you keep it all the way.
q: What do people say about your word or work when they want to name the best?

10.o: Still Solomon looks great, and every thing in this chapter adds to his magnificence. We read nothing indeed of his charity, of no hospitals he built, or alms-houses; he made his kingdom so rich that it did not need them; yet, no question, many poor were relieved from the abundance of his table.
10.s: The Queen of Sheba Comes to See
10.i: The queen of Sheba travels to Jerusalem to test Solomon and leaves convinced that the report is true.
10.p: Lord, Your wisdom is greater than any king's. Lead us to seek it with all our hearts. Amen.
10.l: Ask someone wise a good question today, and listen carefully to the answer.
q: The queen traveled a long way to find wisdom. How far would you go to find it?

11.o: This chapter begins with as melancholy a "but" as almost any we find in all the Bible. Hitherto we have read nothing of Solomon but what was great and good; but the lustre both of his goodness and of his greatness is here sullied and eclipsed, and his sun sets under a cloud. I. The glory of his piety is stained by his departure from God and his duty, in his latter days, marrying strange wives and worshipping strange gods, ver. 4-8. II.
11.i: The wisest king in the Bible ended his reign with divided loyalties, and the writer of Kings names the enemies that grew out of it.
11.p: Lord, keep our hearts whole toward You. When we drift, turn us back before the cost grows. Amen.
11.l: Think of one small thing you keep doing even though you know it pulls you away from what you love. Tell God about it, and ask a grown-up to help you stop.
q: A king with God on his side need fear no adversary, and a king without Him fears the least. What small thing in your life has become a bigger worry because of a drift you have not faced?

12.o: The glory of the kingdom of Israel was in its height and perfection in Solomon; it was long in coming to it, but it soon declined, and began to sink and wither in the very next reign, as we find in this chapter, where we have the kingdom divided, and thereby weakened and made little in comparison with what it had been. Here is, I. Rehoboam's accession to the throne and Jeroboam's return out of Egypt, ver. 1, 2. II.
12.i: Afraid of losing his throne, King Jeroboam set up golden calves at Bethel and Dan, a shortcut religion that kept his people from going to Jerusalem.
12.p: Lord, keep us from shortcuts in worship. Give us hearts that come to You as You are. Amen.
12.l: Notice one thing you do just because it is easier, or because everyone does it, and ask God whether it is really His way.
q: Jeroboam changed worship to protect his own position. What have you made easier or more convenient than God's way?

13.o: In the close of the foregoing chapter we left Jeroboam attending his altar at Beth-el, and there we find him in the beginning of this, when he received a testimony from God against his idolatry and apostasy. This was sent to him by a prophet, a man of God that lived in Judah, who is the principal subject of the story of this chapter, where we are told, I. What passed between him and the new king. 1. The prophet threatened Jeroboam's altar (ver. 1, 2), and gave him a sign (ver.
13.s: The Man of God from Judah
13.i: First Kings 13 is a strange, short story at Bethel about a prophet who spoke the truth and then believed a lie.
13.p: Lord, You speak clearly. Help us to hold to what You have said, even when someone persuasive offers something easier. Amen.
13.l: Ask yourself today if you are listening to what God has said or to someone who says God told them something different.
q: God sent his messenger before the king's heart was hardened. What warning are you hearing now that you would rather put off?

14.o: The kingdom being divided into that of Judah and that of Israel, we must henceforward, in these books of Kings, expect and attend their separate history, the succession of their kings, and the affairs of their kingdoms, accounted for distinctly. In this chapter we have, I. The prophecy of the destruction of Jeroboam's house, ver. 7-16. The sickness of his child was the occasion of it (ver. 1-6), and the death of his child the earnest of it (ver. 17, 18), together with the conclusion of his reign, ver. 19, 20. II.
14.i: First Kings 14 and 15 move quickly through two kings of Judah and a sick child in the north, and show how a household can lose what it tried to disguise.
14.p: Lord, You see through every disguise. Make us honest, and give us leaders who remove what harms and keep what is good. Amen.
14.l: Do something quietly right today even if the people around you are not doing it.
q: They imagined they honored God by dressing up their worship. What do you do for appearances that God did not ask for?

15.o: In this chapter we have an abstract of the history, I. Of two of the kings of Judah, Abijam, the days of whose reign were few and evil (ver. 1-8), and Asa, who reigned well and long, ver. 9-24. II. Of two of the kings of Israel, Nadab the son of Jeroboam, and Baasha the destroyer of Jeroboam's house, ver. 25-34.
15.i: First Kings 14 and 15 move quickly through two kings of Judah and a sick child in the north, and show how a household can lose what it tried to disguise.
15.p: Lord, You see through every disguise. Make us honest, and give us leaders who remove what harms and keep what is good. Amen.
15.l: Do something quietly right today even if the people around you are not doing it.
q: They imagined they honored God by dressing up their worship. What do you do for appearances that God did not ask for?

16.o: This chapter relates wholly to the kingdom of Israel, and the revolutions of that kingdom—many in a little time. The utter ruin of Jeroboam's family, after it had been twenty-four years a royal family, we read of in the foregoing chapter. In this chapter we have, I. The ruin of Baasha's family, after it had been but twenty-six years a royal family, foretold by a prophet (ver. 1-7), and executed by Zimri, one of his captains, ver. 8-14. II. The seven days' reign of Zimri, and his sudden fall, ver. 15-20. III.
16.i: First Kings 16 moves through four kings in a few years, and introduces the pair who would clash with Elijah.
16.p: Lord, You see every throne and every nation. Raise up leaders who fear You, and keep us from compromise. Amen.
16.l: Choose today to do what is right, even when everyone around you is choosing otherwise.
q: Jezebel's influence turned a king into a puppet. Whose voice is steering you more than your own conscience?

17.o: So sad was the character both of the princes and people of Israel, as described in the foregoing chapter, that one might have expected God would cast off a people that had so cast him off; but, as an evidence to the contrary, never was Israel so blessed with a good prophet as when it was so plagued with a bad king. Never was king so bold to sin as Ahab; never was prophet so bold to reprove and threaten as Elijah, whose story begins in this chapter and is full of wonders.
17.i: God hid Elijah by a dry-country stream and fed him by birds nobody would trust with dinner. The brook then dried up, and the next step was waiting.
17.p: Lord, You fed Elijah by the hand of ravens. Teach us to trust You for today's bread, and to be ready for tomorrow's step. Amen.
17.l: Think of one thing you worry about running out of. Tell God about it, and watch for how help might show up, maybe from someone you did not expect.
q: Ravens fed a prophet when God pleased. Where might help reach you from a place you would never expect?

18.o: We left the prophet Elijah wrapt up in obscurity. It does not appear that either the increase of the provision or the raising of the child had caused him to be taken notice of at Zarephath, for then Ahab would have discovered him; he would rather do good than be known to do it.
18.i: On Mount Carmel, Elijah challenges the prophets of Baal to a contest, and God answers with fire and then with rain.
18.p: Lord, You answer by fire and by rain. Make us wholehearted for You. Amen.
18.l: Pray about something that feels impossible, and keep praying and watching.
q: Elijah kept praying and watching until a small cloud appeared. When have you had to pray and wait?

19.o: We left Elijah at the entrance of Jezreel, still appearing publicly, and all the people's eyes upon him. In this chapter we have him again absconding, and driven into obscurity, at a time when he could ill be spared; but we are to look upon it as a punishment to Israel for the insincerity and inconstancy of their reformation. When people will not learn it is just with God to remove their teachers into corners. Now observe, I. How he was driven into banishment by the malice of Jezebel his sworn enemy, ver. 1-3. II.
19.i: Elijah flees from Jezebel to Mount Horeb, where God meets him in a gentle whisper.
19.p: Lord, You speak in the quiet. Help us to listen, and to rest in Your care. Amen.
19.l: Spend a few minutes in silence today, and listen for what God might say.
q: Elijah felt alone, and God said he was not. Who might God be using to remind you that you are not alone?

20.o: This chapter is the history of a war between Ben-hadad king of Syria and Ahab king of Israel, in which Ahab was, once and again, victorious. We read nothing of Elijah or Elishain all this story; Jezebel's rage, it is probable, had abated, and the persecution of the prophets began to cool, which gleam of peace Elijah improved.
20.i: First Kings 20 describes two Aramean invasions that Israel won only because a prophet said God would give the victory, and a treaty Ahab should not have made.
20.p: Lord, You are God of the hills and the valleys. Help us to give You the credit for every victory, and to obey You when we win. Amen.
20.l: Say thank you to God today for a time He helped you when you were outnumbered.
q: Calling in outside help can cost later generations dearly. What shortcut now might cost someone else later?

21.o: Ahab is still the unhappy subject of the sacred history; from the great affairs of his camp and kingdom this chapter leads us into his garden, and gives us an account of some ill things (and ill indeed they proved to him) relating to his domestic affairs. I. Ahab is sick for Naboth's vineyard, ver. 1-4. II. Naboth dies by Jezebel's plot, that the vineyard may escheat to Ahab, ver. 5-14. III. Ahab goes to take possession, ver. 15-16. IV.
21.i: Ahab and Jezebel had Naboth killed so the king could take his vineyard, and Elijah told them that God sees injustice.
21.p: Lord, You defend the powerless and judge the unjust. Make us honest, and forgive us when we take what is not ours. Amen.
21.l: Be honest today with something small that could be taken the easy way. Choose the right way, even when it is harder.
q: Ahab took what he wanted by using power. When are you tempted to take what is not yours?

22.o: This chapter finishes the history of Ahab's reign. It was promised in the close of the foregoing chapter that the ruin of his house should not come in his days, but his days were soon at an end. His war with the Syrians at Ramoth-Gilead is that which we have an account of in this chapter. I. His preparations for that war. He consulted, 1. His privy-council, ver. 1-3. 2. Jehoshaphat, ver. 4. 3. His prophets. (1.) His own, who encouraged him to go on this expedition (ver. 5, 6), Zedekiah particularly, ver. 11, 12.
22.i: First Kings 22 is the story of four hundred yes-men and one honest prophet, and what the difference cost.
22.p: Lord, You speak truth even when it is hard. Give us the courage of Micaiah, and ears to hear what You say. Amen.
22.l: Say something true and kind today, even if people around you want to hear something else.
q: Whose friendship are you leaning on, and what do you give back?
